code.note: Repo ships circles-0.3.2.1/ (Fortran 77 + C) and reproduce_RBG08.sh. Commit seen by scout at fetch time; the rerun mind must confirm the commit it checks out. Paper footnote 7 names circles-0.3.2.1 for the five-year WMAP MCMC; it does not say which version produced Table 1, so this is a caveat.

stack: Fortran 77 (circles, GPL) with a C front end; 2008-era numerical code; 2020 reproduction report was on GNU Fortran 6.3 with GSL 1.10

claim.location: Table 1 (Sect. 4.1, 'Example of benchmarking on a 3GHz processor'), first row group, alpha = 5 deg, r2 = 0.4 h^-1 Gpc, N_p = 1000 (the row with alpha+ = '...', i.e. no preselection)
claim.value_check: Read verbatim from page 5 of the PDF of arXiv:0807.4260 (v2 render), Table 1: row '5 | 0.4 | ... | 1000 | 5 | 1317 | 52'. Columns: alpha (deg), r2 (h^-1 Gpc), alpha+ (deg), N_p, t (s), N_A, N_C. Caption d: numbers of pairs in the smallest bin for xi_A and xi_C.
claim.metric: integer pair counts N_A and N_C in the smallest separation bin for one cross-correlation calculation at a fixed arbitrary PDS orientation and twist, with the paper's fixed pseudo-random seed

tolerance.basis: Fixed before any run: N_A within 10 percent of 1317, N_C within 5 of 52. Timing column t is NOT part of the claim (hardware-dependent). Not to be loosened after any run.

cost.cpu_minutes_estimate: Under 1 minute. Paper's t = 5 s on a 3 GHz processor for this row; a build plus one run is expected to fit well under an hour.
cost.data_size: None. The benchmark is a simulated sky with an arbitrary PDS orientation; no WMAP or other dataset is needed.
cost.caveat: The paper says the pseudo-random generator has the same initial seed for each calculation, but does not state the seed value. If the rerun cannot match the seed, counts may differ and the result must be recorded as such; that is a finding, not a reason to change the tolerance.

why: Older Fortran 77 / C numerical code with a checkable table of integer counts from a single cheap, data-free calculation; the 2008 paper's claim is a benchmark, which tests whether the code still runs and matches its own counts.
